entries.title: She Was a Victim of Jeffrey Epstein. She Also Helped Him Find Other Girls.
entries.summary: "During the four years that Marina Lacerda was abused by Epstein, she introduced him to many of her friends."
entries.content:
During the four years that Marina Lacerda was abused, she introduced Jeffrey Epstein to many of her friends. And they, in turn, did the same with their friends. How do these women live with the anger, guilt, and shame Epstein forced upon them? How do they live with each other? Jen Percy grapples with one of the most painful aspects of Epstein’s legacy:

He tried to pit the girls against one another by comparing them, inciting jealousy. He made comments about their bodies. He would call one on the phone, ignoring the others. He didn’t like the girls getting too close—he had more control when they were fighting for his attention. Sometimes the girls they brought weren’t good enough. He said they looked too tired, too old, too dark or too heavy. Sometimes he’d say they wore too much makeup.

Lisa treated finding girls like a job. She was always thinking, I need to go talk to this girl. Sometimes Lisa brought two or three girls a day. She’s pretty sure she brought the most girls of anyone in Queens, maybe in all of New York and Florida. She felt like it was all day, every day, constantly for at least seven years. She met them everywhere: the nail salon, shopping centers, clubs like Marquee. She knew how to find girls like herself: No parents, no job, drug addiction? Perfect. She figured that was the kind of girl she could help. Lisa would say: “Oh, my god, I love your shoes. Where are you from? What do you do?” And once she heard their story, she would tell them she knew Epstein. She felt like a savior. She was giving young immigrants the chance at the American dream.

entries.title: Dollywood After Dolly: My Pilgrimage to a Grieving Tennessee
entries.summary: "At the park, Parton was known as the dreamer-in-chief. Vanity Fair’s Marisa Meltzer visited after her death to celebrate the dreamer in herself."
entries.content:
Soon after Dolly Parton’s passing, Marisa Meltzer heads to Dollywood, in the heart of Dolly country. Expecting a shared experience of mourning, she finds people reluctant to talk to her. Perhaps it’s simply too soon after Dolly’s death—or perhaps, as Meltzer suggests, it’s because she is “unlike about 50% of the people there,” not wearing “a T-shirt emblazoned with a Bible verse, a military slogan, or a celebration of America’s 250 years.” Instead, she finds Dollywood carrying on as usual, even without its “dreamer-in-chief.”

But more than a museum, Dollywood is an amusement park, and a much bigger one than I had realized. It’s a place where you can stand in line for 45 minutes to buy a corn dog while listening to a four-person singing-and-dancing group in the vein of the Mickey Mouse Club does peppy but half-assed covers of Fleetwood Mac and Van Halen. Looping rollercoasters and water tube rides leave families soaking wet in matching T-shirts commemorating their vacations. Dondre, my colleague and our photographer for this journey, waits probably a full hour to squeeze into a vintage muscle car with me so I can simulate steering around a track. It wasn’t until deep into our wait time that we realize this is a children’s ride. At this point, the two of us notice that, in the sea of people, we are the only ones who are childless, wearing dark colors, and audibly bemoaning that Dollywood is dry. (Parton was not a strict teetotaler, but the park bills itself as assertively family-friendly. “Weapons and alcoholic beverages are not permitted on Dollywood Property” is the only explanation given on its website.) No one else seems to care. The ride is quick, but we are ecstatic, high on refillable Diet Cokes, kettle corn, and driving a car, which neither one of us knows how to do in real life.

“Only a society that willfully believes itself ‘post-racist’ could produce such a queen.”

entries.title: The Lost World of Aquaterra
entries.summary: "Most of human history is waiting to be found. And it’s underwater."
entries.content:
“We can’t grasp the depth of the ocean,” writes Elisa Gabbert, “until we throw a skyscraper down there.” How about the edges of early human civilization? For The Atlantic, Toby Lester offers a fascinating, mildly haunting overview of the underneath—specifically, the “submerged prehistory” buried beneath the oceans, and the researchers salvaging it, bit by bit. Reading, I felt awestruck, not merely for the scale of history that lurks beneath our rising waters but the implications for the future of humanity. “What if archaeologists of the future could study only what remained above sea level, in places that today sit well inland from the coast?” an archaeologist suggests to Lester. It’s a wonder to watch Lester play with the hypothetical, to help us better grasp the depths and imagine their future reach.

The chance to name a giant new Earth feature doesn’t arrive often (Antarctica, one of the most recent additions, began to appear on maps in the 1880s, although the word had been around for centuries), and if that feature happens to be largely invisible, you’re likely to run into difficulties persuading others to go along with your name. Call the feature what you will, but it exists: During the past 20,000 years, huge stretches of formerly inhabited land along the world’s coastal shelves have disappeared underwater, taking with them tens of thousands of years of human history.

Until recently, that is. During the past few decades, artifacts and sites dating back millennia have been found off the coasts of every inhabited continent. A growing number of researchers—geographers, archaeologists, anthropologists, amateur enthusiasts—are turning their attention to what lies offshore. “Everywhere we’ve systematically looked, we’ve found some areas where the former landscape has survived,” Jessi Halligan, an anthropologist at Texas A&M, told me. “And in a lot of those places, those former landscapes have had sites on them.”

Mapping complicated terrain

Have We Been Measuring Mountains All Wrong?

“A new method for quantifying grandeur is reshuffling the pecking order of the planet’s most impressive peaks. Turns out Everest has steep competition.”

How to Map Nothing

“What if we took each sourdough selfie, each Zoom class, each Peloton ride, each Netflix binge and mapped the ecology of resources and services that have made it possible for some of us? And at the same time impossible for others?” On pandemic maps and the Great Pause.

Here Be Dragons: Finding the Blank Spaces in a Well-Mapped World

Maps are how we orient ourselves, and how we donate a place’s value — and by extension, the value of that place’s inhabitance. What does that means for the place still left un-mapped?

entries.title: The Brits Paying To Be Frozen After Death
entries.summary: "Some Brits are betting on life after death. We joined them at cryonics training camp. Will they ever wake up?"
entries.content:
For Dispatch, Chantalle Edmunds joined a dozen people at a Sheffield hotel during a Cryonics UK training event, where they practiced preparing a body for cryopreservation. Among the attendees was Garret Smyth, who became the first person in the UK, 40 years ago, to sign up for the procedure (though he now plans to undergo neuropreservation, which aims to preserve only the brain). Edmunds’s dispatch offers a sense of why some people make this bet, even when their future is not guaranteed.

Gaspar describes her mother’s preservation as a “triumph”. It involved a different process from conventional cryonics. At Sparks Brain Preservation, a non-profit in Salem, Oregon, founded by the former dentist and programmer Jordan Sparks, a chemical compound called aldehyde is used to preserve the structure of the brain instead of traditional cryonics. The rest of Noélia’s body was cremated.

entries.title: What I Learned About Christmas—And Life—By Starring* in a Hallmark Movie
entries.summary: "On a Hallmark movie set, it is always Christmas but rarely winter."
entries.content:
I recently saw a joke: “What has 15 actors, 4 settings, 2 writers, and 1 plot? 646 Hallmark movies.” The humor, of course, lies in the accuracy. Hallmark has been churning out twinkly, sugary romances for years, but what’s it like to be on one of those movie sets? Alexandra Petri finds out firsthand, landing a tiny role in one of this year’s offerings. She fully embraces the fun—and so should you!

But then, in 2006, we got The Christmas Card. This is the Hallmark Christmas blueprint, and it is in every way a perfect film. The stereotypical Hallmark-movie plot can sound a bit dystopian: “She was a busy woman from the big city. Then one day the snow trapped her in Christmasville, and she never left …” The Christmas Card inverts this paradigm. Our protagonist, Faith, already lives in a small town. What’s more, she loves this town, and her job at the family lumber mill, more than anything—a fact that is lost on her absentee city-slicker boyfriend, Paul, an international wine broker in a tiny sports car. But, fortunately, Faith has sent a Christmas card to a soldier named Cody, stationed in Afghanistan, and Cody is so charmed by the card that when he gets a break from fighting the War on Terror, he visits her town. He then saves Faith’s dad from an out-of-control speeding car and starts helping at the lumber business. He also picks her up in a sleigh—with her favorite blanket. Wine Broker Paul does not stand a chance. There’s an exquisite scene where Paul spends two hours in the woods yelling into his cellphone about wine while, behind him, Cody takes down Christmas trees with a chainsaw.

entries.title: In the Doldrums
entries.summary: What does a week in New Mexico without the internet have in common with Moby-Dick?
entries.content:
Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.

Longreads has published hundreds of original stories—personal essays, reported features, reading lists, and more—and more than 14,000 editor’s picks. And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today.

Megan J. Arlett | Longreads | November 17, 2026 | 20 minutes (5,692 words)

We live in a yellow place. Ninety miles from Roswell, New Mexico, and 120 from Lubbock, Texas, there is little in any direction but dairy farms and flat, endless plains. When I take the dogs to the sad excuse for a walking path on the edge of town (next to a field of rusted cars and the dairy plant), I can turn in a circle and see an almost 360-degree view of the horizon. Because it takes so much effort to get anywhere from here, I conceive of it as an island. There is a Walmart and a small local grocery store we call The Best Restaurant in Town because we enjoy the tamales and breakfast burritos at its hot bar. A café called Do Drop Inn serves 12 slightly different variations of a turkey sandwich. There are the staple fast-food chains of any American town: McDonald’s, Burger King, Taco Bell, Domino’s, Sonic. There is just enough to not need to leave to get anything, and not enough to make you want to stay.

The quiet in Portales is like this: the big dog’s light breathing as she sleeps on the guest bed beside my desk, the little dog scratching behind her ear, the air conditioner kicking on, a distant rumble of a car down the street. In the mornings, I rarely see another person walking around the neighborhood. Sometimes, someone steps from their house and waves briefly as they get in their car, but this happens maybe once a week. Mostly it feels like I am walking around a toy town, or a town where something has gone horribly wrong and I am the last person to learn about it.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s The Rime of the Ancient Mariner describes the doldrums as “that silent sea.” In Coleridge’s poem, the breeze drops, the sails turn slack, the sailors speak only to break the silence around them, the sun is hot and copper, and “day after day, day after day, / we stuck, nor breath nor motion: / As idle as a painted ship / Upon a painted ocean.” Sailors call it “the doldrums,” but the band of water five degrees north and south of the equator is actually the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone. Here, where the heat of the equator forces warm air upward, there is little surface wind and the waters can stay calm for weeks. During the age of sailing, boats would languish at the ocean’s mercy until caught by a rogue thread of air a month or so later and sent on their way. In 2003, Bernie Harberts, an author and filmmaker who describes himself as a slow traveler (his goal is not to arrive in a place but to experience the getting there), got stuck in the doldrums purposefully. “I was hung between the sea and sky,” he wrote. In a video he made, with the flat waters on all sides of him, he said, “I feel in many ways like an astronaut or a spaceman out in space.”

In Portales, I am hung between the sky and the yellow-brown, sun-baked earth. I have the tenure-track job I spent eight years in graduate school working toward, a job that feels like a golden ticket snatched from the hands of other people just as (maybe more) deserving of it than I am. But the contrast between the nine months of the year when the university is in session and the three months when it is not still jars me. In the past 10 months I have taught eight classes, overseen the publication of two printed editions of a literary magazine run by students with little experience, directed four master’s theses, audited two classes, traveled to England (a two-hour drive to the airport, a one-hour flight, a layover, a three-hour flight, a layover, a seven-hour flight) to renew my visa, visited family in Spain, got engaged, attempted to plan a wedding, attended two conferences, traveled to Austin, Cloudcroft, Santa Fe, Kansas City, and San Angelo, eaten healthily, worked out five days a week, and walked the dogs every morning despite the little dog reacting aggressively to all other creatures.

Every day I woke dreading what I had to do; the to-do list never shrinking no matter how hard I worked. Every time I cleared out grading, I was lucky to have a day of respite before more arrived. I ate lunch at my desk, responding to emails that had accumulated while I was teaching in the morning. When I returned home in the afternoons, I read the texts I was teaching the next day. Every evening, I ate dinner in front of the television, then sank into a blob on the sofa, a pile with the dogs and the man I love, before getting into bed where my fiancé would run his fingers through my hair, untangling the knots with patience and tenderness. Every night I lay awake beside him for another hour or two, stewing over everything to get done. In some ways, it was a good thing that there was so little to do here. At least I couldn’t feel that I was missing out. What was there to miss out on? (“Is it that by its indefiniteness it shadows forth the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and thus stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation, when beholding the white depths of the Milky Way?” asks Ishmael.) In my end-of-year review, I was told I am “exceeding expectations,” but should continue to look for ways to expand how I serve the university.

Time at sea is either dull or so full of the actions needed to stay alive you can’t think. In Moby-Dick, Ishmael describes his desire to join the crew of The Pequod as a “sort of brief interlude and solo between more extensive performances.” Herman Melville based many of his novels on his own experiences as a merchant sailor—the five years he spent at sea in his early twenties that left him with a “hatred of external authority” and “a lust for personal freedom.” I have longed for the freedoms of summer, but when it arrives I am stretched so thin, so exhausted, so over every aspect of my work that I slump into the break with no ability to do the writing I have thought about and longed for since the previous August, the writing I am convinced is my ticket out of this place. The doldrums are a term for a funk, the blues. But by most measures I am the happiest I have ever been. Together, we earn double the average state income. For the first time in our adult lives, we have money to spend on shit like pizza ovens and quality leather shoes and all the books that have been on my “Want to Read” list for years. We take naps together and wake up pressed into each other’s warm bodies. More than that, every day the little glowing bud in my chest grows larger, not a mote of uncertainty about this life we are building together.

For the first month of summer I am over-cooked, under-seasoned, a disgrace. I want to loaf and lounge, to wake up early and walk, return home and, after closing the door behind me, not leave the house again. I want to boil the kettle, make tea and settle in to do the things I love: writing, reading, drawing, painting, napping. Instead, day after day, I sit down at my desk and scroll the internet. The morning dissolves into a thick slop of webpages, so many I can barely remember what I have read. Lunch arrives, and I am irritable at having achieved nothing. I break away from my laptop and reach for my phone, and like a coding sequence I cannot escape, open Instagram or TikTok, then 30 minutes later shake myself out of the same loop. I feel the days slip by, egg whites through my fingers. By the time mid-June hits, I am bubbling with anxiety and irritation at all the things I have not done because it is easier to consume this brief and vapid content than it is to sit down and create art. I have no ideas. I have no focus. Even when I get to the page, what comes out has no substance. All the bright, colorful creations I planned months ago when I was too busy to do them have evaporated into the edgelessness of summer. In the mornings, I look over at my fiancé and his index finger flipping through 30-second video after 30-second video. “That’s got to be bad for your brain,” I say to him—as though I hadn’t been doing the same thing moments before.

I can feel myself changing as I fixate on everything I am dissatisfied with. I can feel myself pushing on the walls of my worked-for, wanted life—yet there are no walls. The horizon is all there is. I decide I must shake myself awake by journeying into my own silent sea. I must enter the metaphorical doldrums to exit the very real ones. I will cut myself off from the internet for a week. Just a week. Like turning it on and off again. The “it” being me. I prepare to enter the doldrums as though I am about to embark on a long journey. I respond to emails, download the articles I want to read, check tabs to make sure I don’t forget anything urgent. And then, more tentatively than I thought given my initial excitement, I disconnect Wi-Fi from my laptop, delete apps from my phone, and push off from the shore.

The first 24 hours in the doldrums are not as clean a cut as I had planned. The Safari app on my phone cannot be deleted, and the option to cap time spent on it is easily worked around by pressing a button that says, “Fifteen more minutes.” Then I remember I haven’t deleted TikTok off my phone, which leads to 35 minutes of just-one-last-video. Finally, I unhook myself, delete the app, and stare at the wall. I imagined my “trip,” as I was conceiving it, would be revelatory, that I would step immediately into a new life where I could prioritize doing the things I love without the constant humming pull of the internet. Instead, the first few hours look like this: I make myself a coffee, I read 15 pages of a good book of poetry but keep picking up my phone like there’s something more important there (there isn’t; nobody has texted), I start to work through the tabs I have accumulated on my laptop and actually read the things I have been hoarding. I read 22 pages of a terrible book of poetry and wonder how it even got recommended to me; I put on some laundry, find my Kindle, and open another long-neglected book. Propped against the kitchen table is a whiteboard with the title “Wedding To-Do” scrawled in blue ink.

My fiancé had proposed six months earlier on the balcony of my grandparents’ home in England. Within hours of becoming engaged, our families and friends began asking when the wedding would be. Of course, we had thought about it all in theory, spun out a dream elopement: a small cabin in the woods with a handful of friends. Quiet. Intimate. But over dinner the night of our engagement, my mother and stepfather offered us enough money toward a wedding that we had to consider what it would mean to our families. Planning this wedding became a knot of thought that consumed me. It also made me angry at the man who, just 48 hours before, had asked me to marry him. “We’re thinking of this July,” he mentioned casually to my uncle. I looked at the two of them with wide eyes. “We are?” I asked, knowing wedding venues like the ones we were hoping for (beautiful, affordable, near major airports) book out 18 months in advance, knowing my family must fly internationally, knowing we don’t even have a solid budget yet.

The algorithm had already been pushing engagement and wedding content my way for months, and, of course, I consumed it. “Ten things I wish I knew before my wedding,” “Tips from a wedding photographer,” and “Dresses I didn’t choose part 8.” I was a diligent servant of the wedding industry. When my fiancé said, “I think we can have the kind of wedding we want for $10,000,” I scoffed and huffed about the house. I pulled up the website of the only venue I had found that fit what we wanted and pointed out that booking started at $8,500 before any catering or drinks. Even as I was doing this, I knew I was being a bitch about it all. I was angry he didn’t know. I was angry I was the one expected to know. I was angry nobody asked him about the wedding, that all the questions were directed at me. I was angry my whole life had socialized me to know about wedding dress alterations, floral arrangements, and “cost per plate,” and my fiancé, who in all other aspects of our lives felt like my mirror and equal, thought we could find a “good enough” photographer for less than $1,000. “Maybe a student?” he suggested before I schooled him on why we would not be doing that. Every night I lay awake until two or three in the morning, turning over logistics in my mind, wondering how we would pay for it all, how I would pull it together when I had so much else to do. After days of this, I finally admitted the swirling anxieties keeping me up, and he suggested we put a stay on wedding talk. No planning or discussions for a month. Not until February. I could work with this.

Day two in the doldrums, and the yucca along the sidewalks have bloomed into tall coral towers over the last month. It’s 8:30 a.m. on a Tuesday and a single car passes me the entirety of my walk with the dogs. A man stands outside his property talking on the phone. I lift my hand in a gesture of acknowledgement. He meets my eye and ignores me. When people hear we live in New Mexico, they often say, “The desert is so beautiful!” But we don’t live in the desert. Instead, we live on the high plains, a place I tell people is—somehow—the only ugly part of this state. In the late 19th century, a small water source on the high plains served as a resting point for travelers making their way through the area, and the rocky bluffs where they would camp for the night had small alcoves that looked a little like the front porches of houses in Mexico called portales. In the book I took out from the library about the town’s history, I am amused to find that most people ended up here by accident. A broken axle on the covered wagon or a sick child needing care in the only town for 200 treeless miles. There is no spring-fed lake here anymore. The trains no longer stop. In the spring, wind storms pull across the flat landscape and fill the air with red-brown dust, blotting out the sun.

The downtown has burned to the ground twice in the last 100 years, and as I drive to get groceries, I pass abandoned storefronts and more yards filled with trash and stripped-down vehicles than not. The dairies that surround town have drained the water table, and whoever runs social media at the fire station tells us levels are too low for them to use hydrants if they need to. The distinct stench of cow manure wafts over town most days. As the weather heats up, flies invade our house in droves, and we dodge the strings of sticky traps we must hang throughout the kitchen and garage, catching dozens a day. I try to find beauty in this life here. My happy life with this person I love, our pets, our walls full of art and bookshelves.

Melville left sailing a 25-year-old resentful outsider, but I don’t want to settle for being aggrieved. This is not Ishmael’s interlude. This is not the intermission of my life. I want to wake up. The week before setting sail, my daily phone usage was four-and-a-half hours a day. Already, this has halved. I spend time texting friends and family and replace scrolling online with scrolling through photos: photos of the dogs playing, recipes I never made, images of museum exhibits, endlessly similar but somehow totally different wedding dresses from earlier in the year when I had been in a city where I could actually try some on.

After wedding discussions were back on the table, it had taken a single night of sleepless anxiety for us to make a decision. “I can’t be like this for another year and a half,” I told my fiancé as we ate lunch in the campus cafeteria. “I don’t want you to be like this for another year and a half,” he admitted. He is always so calm (“an intense copper calm, like a universal yellow lotus”), and while I know a little pair of duck feet paddle under the surface, he keeps it all under control so much better than I do. We make a decision: We would have the small elopement we originally planned with six friends that summer in Santa Fe, and small receptions with our respective families afterward. Everyone would be happy.

Day three, I wake up groggy. A touch too much alcohol the night before on a touch too little for dinner, combined with staying up too late with each other after we came home. The night before at the bar (the only open bar on a weeknight), I laugh about the premise of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner with a colleague who specializes in 19th-century British literature. “He just grabs some poor guy at a wedding and holds him hostage to hear his story!” (“An ancient Mariner meeteth three Gallants bidden to a wedding-feast, and detaineth one,” writes Coleridge.) Then, I hold her hostage to tell her about my own adventure into the Land of No Internet. I tell her that when I finally make it off the island that is Portales and tell people about my plight, I feel like the same haggard, wild-eyed sailor on the edges of the party. “It’s terrible,” I complain to whoever meanders within my reach. “I have to escape.” I remind myself of the scene in Mean Girls where Cady can hear people getting bored with her but cannot stop herself. My complaints bubble at all times.

Day three returns my feverish ability to read. As a child, my grandmother picked my birthday gift books based on length, knowing anything fewer than 300 pages would be finished so quickly it was barely worth buying. Slowly, slowly, my reading lessened as my hours on the computer increased. But I remember the day I spent on the swinging lounger on the back patio reading A Thousand Splendid Suns from cover to cover, barely pausing to eat or pee. Every few years as an adult, I found a book that consumed me like this, but it has become increasingly rare. My work is so focused on books and writing that slowly, slowly I lost the ability to be absorbed. My brain is always working to connect to something else or find a kernel of inspiration. My fingers always reaching across the sofa toward my phone.

Growing up in England, there wasn’t enough television programming to get lost in it for hours. We had four channels: BBC 1, BBC 2, ITV, Channel 4, and maybe Channel 5 if we toyed around with the antenna enough. I came home from school, and BBC 1 had children’s programming from 3:15 until 5 p.m. Then I had to keep myself busy until dinner and into the rest of the evening. When I told my students this, they looked at me like they couldn’t decide if I was too foreign to make sense of or whether I had grown up wearing bonnets. They have been perpetually online their entire lives, whereas my life straddled a change in the ether. In the doldrums, I want to reclaim something lost from before.

All afternoon while my fiancé watches a documentary about the previous year’s Tour de France, I sit with my legs slung over his lap, his hands tracing lazy circles on the skin of my thighs. Being with him is as good as being alone. Sometimes we take turns lying with our ears pressed to each other’s stomachs and mimic the gurgles we hear until we’re laughing too hard to keep going. Sometimes when I’m working, he will walk into my office, spin my chair around, squeeze my face until I’m puckered like a fish, kiss me, and then scurry off without a word. On day three, sitting with him in silence, I read. I am now juggling two books of poetry, an audiobook, two novels, plus a return to Moby-Dick, which mostly involves rereading whale facts and the chapter with the mothers and calves. Why can’t you just be normal? The meme from The Babadook rings through my head. Everything comes back to the internet.

The internet doesn’t want to let go. In the middle of the day, I become convinced an important email is waiting for me in my inbox. I’ll just check it quickly. And I do. I turn Wi-Fi back on, open my inbox, and find nothing but sales emails and a reminder that my credit card will autopay at the end of the week. I convince myself that because it wasn’t fruitful, it hardly counted as a break in my endeavor. How do we begin to comprehend the vastness of the internet, of its hold? How big is the internet? If I weren’t in the doldrums, I would Google this. Instead, I turn back to the physical pages littering my desk. Is the internet as “immense as whales, the motion of whose vast bodies can in a peaceful calm trouble the ocean till it boil”? Is the internet a wide and endless water, a fathomless sea? “He smites his chest,” whispered Stubb, “what’s that for? Methinks it rings most vast, but hollow.” Vast, but hollow.

Three-and-a-half years ago, before New Mexico, before my fiancé, before the little dog, I woke up in Texas to a blue light. The light that fills a house after snowfall, bright and half a shade of unexpected. The night before, as I wandered through the grocery store, I had noticed the things people hadn’t stocked up on before the storm: red onions, celery, baby potatoes. It would be unusually cold, the weather apps on our phones told us. The next morning, when I got out of bed to turn on the coffee maker, the air was chilled and silent. In the hallway, I checked the thermostat: 50 degrees. The quiet of the house turned strange. No lights. No hum of heating. In the kitchen I pressed the button to make the coffee and nothing happened. We had no electricity. Outside, the air was -9 degrees Fahrenheit. Inside, the temperature was dropping. From the storage container under my bed, I extracted my thermal leggings and ski jacket. I layered up. The big dog was curled up in a tight knot. Her ears were cold. I put two blankets around her. I unwrapped the electric blanket I hadn’t used in years and put it between two layers of quilts. If the electricity came back on, I would make a warmth sandwich for us. Not only was there no electricity, but no cell service. No way to know how long this might last or what was coming.

On the first day, the electricity cycled on and off unreliably. Forty-five minutes on, an hour and thirty off. An hour and five on, an hour and fifteen off. I curled up in bed with the dog tucked beside me under the blankets and read books one after the other, ploughing through my to-read list. My bed, a small raft we were safe in. Elsewhere in the state, people died in their homes and cars from the cold. I drifted in and out of light sleep, waking each time the hallway light lit up so I could turn the electric blanket back on. For three days I mostly stayed in bed. I read endlessly, escaping to different worlds, pouring through pages, gaining momentum as I went, disrupted from time and space.

By day four in the doldrums in New Mexico, I notice time slips by differently. I am more engaged with my work. I watch the clock less. I am no longer counting down to lunchtime. I add a wash of light yellow to the painting I am working on, water the plants, then pull a load of laundry from the dryer. I eat lunch silently at the living room table instead of in front of the TV. I am still convinced an email that will change my life is waiting for me in my inbox, but I resist checking. I work out in the garage lifting weights and, between sets, instead of sitting on the bench scrolling, I walk out into the garden and rile the dogs up so I can watch them chase each other. Small white cabbage butterflies rise from the grass.

Of course, I feel a little superior now that I have cut myself off from the internet. I lay in bed. My fiancé scrolls through videos beside me. I do a crossword or conjugate Spanish verbs in the workbook I bought myself and sometimes, if the video he is watching sounds particularly interesting, I peer over his shoulder to catch a glimpse. “It doesn’t count as being off the internet if you’re just watching it on my phone instead,” he tells me, continuing to swipe at the screen. During the semester, the internet on campus is unreliable. If it rains or snows, it will undoubtedly go down. Half of my classes are “hybrid synchronous,” meaning that half of my students are in the room with me on campus and half attend virtually via Zoom. During these hours, I would give anything to return to a time without Wi-Fi. The university does not pay for the Zoom accounts we need to hold our classes, nor does it provide the microphones we need so our 15 students can hear each other reliably. My discussion classes become an echoing exercise in repeating what has just been said so everyone can hear it. I come home exhausted from the dance. I sit on the sofa and long to teach in a way that doesn’t feel like trying to hold my head above water.

On day five, an unseasonably heavy sky sits over town, a gray, undulating blanket. I sleep deeply. I wake to the big dog whining for breakfast. I drink coffee. I walk the dogs and turn on the UV light I am using to help the struggling mint plant flourish. I strain a batch of yogurt. I work on a small watercolor I plan to give to a friend. I write about the doldrums. I heat up leftovers for lunch. I unload the dishwasher. At the end of the street we live on, I look out over the vast lake of dried-out grasses that stretches out until the curvature of the earth takes it from sight. (“Starbuck himself was seen coolly and adroitly balancing himself to the jerking tossings of his chip of a craft, and silently eyeing the vast blue eye of the sea.”) In the far distance, the top half of wind turbines pass in semi-circles over the horizon like whales breaching, and I remember with a pulse the chapter in Moby-Dick where the crew of The Pequod finds themselves sailing through yellow instead of blue. They are parting a path through brit, a species of krill. “For leagues and leagues it undulated round us,” Ishmael writes. “So that we seemed to be sailing through boundless fields of ripe and golden wheat.”

Life on whaling ships often passed with weeks or months between whale sightings, and the crew entertained themselves with the routines of keeping the ship ready: washing the deck, setting the sails, steering, keeping watch. These days were better than the drama-filled ones, although less interesting to read about. Logbooks contain accounts of mutinies, desertions, women stowaways, drunkenness, scurvy, collisions, fire, hurricanes, men falling from the masthead, and ships crushed by ice. Summers in Portales pass in a haze of routine. Though we have lived in this yellow place for almost two years, two weeks ago more rain arrived than we had ever seen here; the back garden suddenly choked with knee-high green grass and weeds. As close to drama as we get.

Day six. The air is filled with humidity. Again, strange. At the walking path—full of weeds, strewn with trash, marked with rusted metal nets from when this used to be a disc golf course—we pass the same middle-aged man almost every morning. He always walks three loops of the path before returning to his truck, where he trades his walking shoes for leather work boots. He always says hello to me in a thick Mexican accent, points to the dogs, and says, “Let them run!” And every time I respond by pointing to the little dog tethered firmly to a band at my waist, then the horizon, and saying, “She’d be gone forever!” This is only a slight exaggeration. The little dog drives forward like a natural disaster, diving into bushes after lizards and snatching up random crud from the ground. Walking the two dogs at the same time is an activity of extremes. The big dog has been an old soul since the day I brought her home from the shelter, shivering with nerves. She walks more slowly than you think a dog can. She likes to stop and smell things with a poet’s intensity, pause, and look at the sky.

Day seven. During the summer, my fiancé works in his office on campus while I work in mine at home (a place of chaos filled with paintings and haphazard piles of books that are always threatening to tip into pools on the floor). I am working. I am writing. I am feverish with the reclamation of it all. When he comes home at the end of the day, I feel full of excitement like a dog, thumping her tail against the floor. He’s home! He’s home! All of us rush to the front door when we hear him pull into the driveway. He brings home bags of groceries, plans elaborate meals, slices onions and peppers. I admire how he is a follower of recipes. Disconnecting from my spiralling self long enough to actually enjoy celebrating how much we adore each other has been the albatross around my neck for months. But the list on the “Wedding To-Do” whiteboard is dwindling. Pants adjustments, find shoes, buy tie, vows, ceremony script, flowers. I am almost (almost) looking forward to fulfilling this strange social script.

The doldrums are only a small strip around the belly of the globe. (This period of time, a small strip around the belly of my life, perhaps.) The Pacific and the Atlantic have little interest in being placid, calm things. In 1741, the British warship, The Wager, was believed lost at sea off the top of South America. When two ragged groups of survivors washed ashore, they had become as wild as the sea that had devoured them and spat them out, with conflicting accounts of what had happened. Their words, fought over in court and published in newspapers, caught the attention of Herman Melville as he sat down to write a great American novel about the sea in which he described whales as majestic and significant beings, only to be seen “in unfathomable waters,” and that to hoist a creature like a whale out of the water and to look at one in the air was not to truly see it, since its “mighty swells and undulations” were supposed to be viewed in their element. I want to be in my element. I want to do my best work.

In the last week I have written more than in the last year: poems and vignettes and a long, meandering essay I can’t quite describe. I cannot stay in this internet-free sea indefinitely, but I am not sure how to step back into my life with modesty, how to find something between the all and the nothing. Seven days in the doldrums and I don’t want to leave yet. Even Coleridge’s ancient mariner, who once saw the creatures of the sea as “slimy things,” starts to come around to the ocean’s beauty. Tomorrow I will turn on Wi-Fi and my inbox will refresh. There will be emails to send, calls for submissions to answer, articles to download from databases, texts about “How is wedding planning going?” to respond to with grace and self-deprecation. In these doldrums, forced to spend more time doing and making than yearning for where I am not, I have had to decide what this place will make of me, what version of myself will be spit up on the shore once I make it out the other side. This final night, I take myself out into the back garden where the dogs are chasing each other, kicking up clouds of dirt. Heavy purple-bottomed clouds sink over the high plains, and I can see flashes of dry lightning miles out where the wind farms clip the curvature of the earth.

“Back to real life tomorrow?” my fiancé asks as the little dog narrowly misses crashing into his shins.

“Yeah.”

“How do you feel about it?”

“Not so bad,” I reply, and for the first time in a long time, I don’t think it’s a lie.

Megan J. Arlett was born in the UK, grew up in Spain, and now lives in New Mexico. Her work has appeared in Best New Poets, Best New British and Irish Poets, Gulf Coast, The Kenyon Review, New England Review, Prairie Schooner, The Sun, and Virginia Quarterly Review. Her first book, The Garden Party, is forthcoming with Northwestern University Press in March 2027.

entries.title: Alysa Liu Feels It All
entries.summary: The figure skating phenom took an unconventional path to Olympic gold. Now she’s once again upending expectations — by staying true to herself.
entries.content:
There’s no wrong way into LIFE Magazine‘s first proper new issue in almost 20 years, a relaunch powered by more than 100 contributors and lively with photo-forward features. There are moving interviews with Paralympic powerlifter Garrison Redd and Chris Bledsoe, a North Carolina man who communes with mysterious apparitions, each richly complemented by portraits (by Melchizedek Gayle and Walker Bankson, respectively). There’s the great Stacey Kranitz, snapping away alongside Mesha Maren in a dispatch from West Virginia coal country. Whatever your path, stick the landing with Bonnie Tsui’s profile of Alysa Liu, the Olympic figure skating gold medalist who, at 21, has shaped her own dynamic with her chosen sport by walking away when she must and returning when she wishes. (Nice photos, too, by some guy named Spike Jonze.)

Women’s figure skating is the marquee event of every Winter Olympics. In the world of elite competitive sports, it isn’t alone in having a history of prioritizing winning over well-being, but it has a special reputation for cruelty. As with gymnastics, the physics of ice skating favors youth and a high strength-to-weight ratio; girls are especially vulnerable to body-shaming and social pressures. Eating disorders are a known problem. The tendency toward perfectionism and emotional stoicism — and toward keeping injuries hidden — is long-established.

In this quietly conformist culture, the fact that someone would abandon a meteoric rise sent a shock wave through the sport. But to Liu, that was exactly the point. She was 16, and she had come to hate skating.

entries.title: Crime Pays: How ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Became a Cultural Colossus
entries.summary: “Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art.”
entries.content:
The idea of a hotly anticipated video game isn’t new, but the runup to Grand Theft Auto VI certainly seems unprecedented. It’s been 13 years since the last title in the massive open-world franchise, and the cultural appetite is undeniable. The game’s “extended reveal” crashed Netflix’s servers in August. Other video games’ sales are suffering because of it. NBA fans joke that this week will feature lethargic games and questionable injury reports—all because athletes will have stayed up all night playing GTA VI. For The Guardian, Christian Donlan talks to developers, fans, and critics to get a handle on what exactly makes the Rockstar Games series such a juggernaut.

In the run up to its release, it is easy to focus on the game’s lavish variety, but to say that you can simply do a lot of things in GTA these days – sky-diving, off-road racing, manning your own taxi cab, annoying alligators – is increasingly missing the point. The point instead lies with the density of every frame: the fuzzy edges of exposed drywall in an apartment that has been hastily refitted as a drug den, the brisk splatter of blood that appears on paintwork when someone’s face collides with it. And it goes beyond these vivid details into the realms of things you may only vaguely be aware of. Fly over the mountains in GTA V and the game delivers turbulence in little bursts of haptic feedback through the controller. You may not even notice it, but afterwards you might notice its absence in other games. They don’t pull you into their worlds as convincingly.

entries.title: One Woman’s Fight to Free Herself From a Mental Hospital
entries.summary: "First there was the cancer, then the devastating breakup, and finally came the breakdown. Millie Kerr sought help at one of America’s top psychiatric institutions. It turned into a nightmare."
entries.content:
Millie Kerr wasn’t in great shape when her father convinced her to check in to Houston’s Menninger Clinic. Anxious, distraught, possibly paranoid. But a few days of rest at a well-regarded mental health facility, one whose board her father had served for years, could make a world of difference. She decided when she walked in, and she could decide when she walked out. Right? Not so fast. Mimi Swartz’s feature is one of the most frightening things I’ve read all year—not because the scenario is so outlandish, but because it’s so possible.

In multiple interviews with nurses that day, Millie denied any suicidal ideation whatsoever, asserting that the events of the past week had been “incredibly traumatic.” (She described them to me later as “a perfect storm” of harrowing events that included the surgery, recovery, the fear her cancer had come back, and the breakup with her partner.) According to her medical records, Millie was cooperative, but her near obsession with being allowed to leave at any time was noted; she was, as the nurse wrote, “Hesitant to admit.”

Millie thought a stay of two or three days would be enough for rest and evaluation; the nurse, in contrast, wrote in the file that five to six weeks might be needed to assess and stabilize Millie for unspecified anxiety disorder and an unspecified depressive disorder.
